title: Our solar system and the birth of stars
cards: A system inside a galaxy

Our solar system contains one star, the Sun, eight planets, dwarf planets and natural satellites such as moons orbiting planets. The solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy. A galaxy is not another name for one solar system.
Gravity forms a protostar

The Sun formed from a nebula of gas and dust drawn together by gravity. As the cloud contracts, temperature and pressure rise. A hot protostar forms; when conditions permit, hydrogen fusion begins in the core. Fusion is a nuclear process, not chemical burning.
A stable main-sequence star

Energy from fusion supports an outward effect against gravitational collapse. A stable main-sequence star has a balance between inward gravity and outward pressure effects associated with fusion energy. This is a dynamic energy-producing state, not a star with no forces.
Place an object in the hierarchy

Choose a planet/moon and its orbit centre. Predict whether that is the stated natural relationship. The orbit animation is a teaching diagram: planet sizes, separations and periods are independently exaggerated; the star-formation process uses a separate time scale.

title: Stellar life cycles and new elements
cards: Mass sets the pathway

A star’s life cycle depends on its initial mass. Both pathways begin nebula → protostar → main sequence. Fusion builds heavier nuclei from lighter ones and releases energy in the stages considered here. A star does not become a planet when its fuel changes.
A Sun-sized star

After its main-sequence phase a Sun-sized star expands into a red giant. It sheds outer layers, leaving a hot dense white dwarf that cools. The GCSE pathway describes a later black dwarf; the universe is not yet old enough for white dwarfs to have cooled fully to such objects.
A much more massive star

A high-mass star becomes a red supergiant, then undergoes a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole depending on the remnant. Fusion in stars produces nuclei up to iron in the GCSE account; supernova processes produce heavier elements and disperse elements into space. Detailed modern neutron-star-merger nucleosynthesis is beyond the required model.

Select a Sun-like/high-mass star and an endpoint candidate. Predict whether it matches that pathway. A branching animated timeline shows the two sequences; spacing and playback times are symbolic, not relative stellar lifetimes or a forecast for a particular observed star.

title: Gravity and orbital motion
cards: Gravity keeps an orbit turning

Gravity provides the inward force that maintains a planet or satellite’s circular orbit. The object’s velocity is tangent to the path while the force points toward the centre. It is continuously falling toward the central body rather than needing an outward thrust to balance gravity.
Natural and artificial satellites

Planets orbit their star; moons are natural satellites orbiting planets; artificial satellites are human-made objects placed in orbit. The same gravitational interaction applies. Real orbits can be elliptical; this lesson uses circular paths to isolate the direction account.
Separate speed and direction

A stable circular path can have constant speed while the velocity direction changes. There is therefore an inward acceleration. It is not correct to draw gravity tangentially forward or to claim that orbiting means gravity has disappeared. Higher students must explain this velocity change explicitly.
Predict the inward direction

Choose a satellite at the right/top position of a circular orbit and the centre marker. Predict gravity’s direction. The loop keeps an inward force arrow and tangent velocity arrow distinct. Radius, period and body sizes are symbolic; no inverse-square calculation is required.

extra.title: Higher: stable speed and radius
extra.text: In a circular orbit, gravity changes velocity direction while speed can stay constant. For a stable orbit around the same body, changing the orbital speed requires a change of orbital radius. Lower circular orbits have higher orbital speeds than higher circular orbits. A thrust/change of speed at one point can initially produce a noncircular path; do not infer instant movement to another circle. No orbital-speed equation is required here.

title: Redshift, expansion and the Big Bang
cards: Compare spectral features

Light from most distant galaxies has spectral lines shifted to longer wavelengths compared with matching reference lines measured nearby. This is redshift. It does not mean every galaxy looks visibly red or that all wavelengths have the same numerical change. The pattern of matching lines identifies the comparison.
A distance–recession pattern

More distant galaxies generally show larger redshift and greater recession speeds. This supports expansion of space itself, rather than a special explosion centre located at Earth. A stretching-grid model separates points as the grid expands; points need not grow with the spacing.
Evidence and open questions

Expansion supports the Big Bang model: the universe began in an extremely hot dense state in a very small region. Observations of supernovae since1998 suggest accelerating expansion. Dark matter (called dark mass in the specification) and dark energy remain incompletely understood. Scientists develop and revise theories from observations; the model is not a complete explanation of everything.
Measure a supplied shift

Choose a reference wavelength and an observed increase; predict observed wavelength. The animation separates matching spectral markers while the galaxy grid spacing grows. It is a qualitative teaching analogy, not a full cosmological redshift–distance/time calculation.
